note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in NC.json, gathered 2026-10-04 (mostly the NCDOT guidebook, page-anchored).

byways.name: Airlie Road
byways.where: Airlie Rd from US 76 to the Wrightsville Beach drawbridge (1.5 miles); New Hanover County

facts.fact: The road runs under pines and Spanish moss-covered oaks and opens onto marsh grass and docks on the Intracoastal Waterway.
Airlie Gardens covers 67 acres and holds an oyster roast on Bradley Creek, a tradition since 1905.
The Minnie Evans Bottle Chapel, built of reused glass bottles, honors the folk artist who kept the Airlie gate from 1948 to 1974.

byways.name: Alligator River Route
byways.where: NC 94 from New Holland across Lake Mattamuskeet to Columbia, then US 64 through Alligator and Manns Harbor to Roanoke Island (70.7 miles); Hyde, Tyrrell and Dare counties

facts.fact: The NC 94 causeway runs nearly six miles across Lake Mattamuskeet, the state's largest natural lake, which is only about five feet deep.
The old Mattamuskeet pumping plant, built in failed attempts to drain the lake, is now a wildlife observation tower.
Columbia was founded in the early 1700s as a trading post on the Scuppernong River.

byways.name: Appalachian Medley
byways.where: NC 209 from I-40 Exit 24 near Lake Junaluska through Luck and Trust to Hot Springs, then US 25/70 to Walnut; Haywood and Madison counties

facts.fact: Trust, a mile or so past Luck, is a small community with a general store and cafe.
North of Betsy's Gap the byway follows Spring Creek.
Hot Springs was a drovers' stop, had the first golf course in the Southeast, and the Appalachian Trail runs through the town.

byways.name: Averasboro Battlefield Byway
byways.where: NC 82 (Burnett Rd) from Godwin through the Averasboro battlefield (5.5 miles); Cumberland and Harnett counties

facts.fact: The road follows the route of Sherman's march north of Fayetteville through one of the Civil War's last battlefields; Lafayette traveled it in 1825.
A re-creation of the original trench lines is visible near the county line, followed by the Chicora Civil War Cemetery.
The red roof of Lebanon Plantation, a Confederate hospital, can be seen in a grove about a mile past the museum.

byways.name: Big Horse Creek Byway
byways.where: NC 194 from Warrensville to Lansing, then Big Horse Creek Rd and Rip Shin Rd to the Virginia line (17.9 miles, partly gravel); Ashe County

facts.fact: The byway follows Big Horse Creek into Lansing and crosses it many times.
Part of Rip Shin Rd and Whenlin Ridge Rd is gravel.
Lansing grew with the Virginia-Carolina Railroad, the slow Creeper, built 1914 to 1916; the line closed in 1977.

byways.name: Birkhead Wilderness Route
byways.where: High Pines Church Rd to Lassiter Mill Rd, with an extension on Pisgah Covered Bridge Rd from Ulah; Randolph County

facts.fact: The Birkhead Mountain Wilderness covers over 5,100 acres of the Uwharrie National Forest.
The Pisgah Covered Bridge, built in 1911 for $40, spans 51 feet over the west fork of the Little River and is one of two public covered bridges left in the state.
Old homesteads, crumbling chimneys and gold-mining traces remain in the wilderness.

byways.name: Black Mountain Rag
byways.where: NC 9 south from Black Mountain to Bat Cave, then US 64/74A through Chimney Rock and Lake Lure, with a spur to Edneyville; Buncombe, Henderson and Rutherford counties

facts.fact: The byway takes its name from an old fiddle tune, the Black Mountain Rag.
Bat Cave, on the curves of NC 9, is named for a nearby cave inhabited by bats.
Chimney Rock is a weathered granite monolith overlooking Hickory Nut Gorge and Lake Lure; Hickory Nut Falls drops more than 400 feet.

byways.name: Blue Ridge Parkway
byways.where: 252 NC miles along the Blue Ridge crest from the Virginia line past Boone, Blowing Rock and Asheville to Cherokee; 17 counties

facts.fact: The parkway runs 252 miles in North Carolina, part of 469 miles linking Shenandoah and Great Smoky Mountains national parks.
Construction began in 1935 under the New Deal; the last mile, around Grandfather Mountain, was completed during the Reagan administration.
The route has 26 tunnels, and its highest elevation, at Richland-Balsam Gap, is more than 6,000 feet.

byways.name: Blue-Gray Byway
byways.where: Devils Racetrack Rd from Four Oaks past Bentonville Battlefield, then back roads through Grantham, Seven Springs and Deep Run to Trenton (84 miles); Johnston, Wayne, Lenoir and Jones counties

facts.fact: The byway starts on Devils Racetrack Road, where legend says the hoofbeats of the devil's horse could be heard.
The Battle of Bentonville, March 19-21, 1865, was the largest land battle fought in North Carolina, with nearly 5,000 casualties.
The Seven Springs Hotel was the center of a Victorian mineral springs resort from 1881 to 1944.

byways.name: Brunswick Town Road
byways.where: Orton Rd, Plantation Rd and St. Philips Rd from NC 133 to Brunswick Town/Fort Anderson (2.3 miles); Brunswick County

facts.fact: Brunswick Town, settled in 1725, was a primary colonial port and has been in ruins since 1830.
The ruins of St. Philip's Anglican Church, built in 1751, are surrounded by the Civil War earthworks of Fort Anderson.
Alligators sometimes sun near the road by Orton Plantation.

byways.name: Cape Fear Historic Byway
byways.where: A 10.5-mile loop through downtown Wilmington via Front, Water, 3rd and 5th streets and Greenfield Park; New Hanover County

facts.fact: Wilmington, incorporated in 1739, keeps its original street grid finalized in 1743.
The route passes 1898 Memorial Park, which marks the 1898 overthrow of the city's elected biracial government.
The battleship U.S.S. North Carolina rests across the river from the Riverwalk.

byways.name: Carolina Bay Lakes Byway
byways.where: NC 242 from near Spiveys Corner through Salemburg and Roseboro to Elizabethtown (38.2 miles); Sampson, Cumberland and Bladen counties

facts.fact: Jones, White and Singletary lakes and Lake Waccamaw are Carolina Bays, oval depressions once thought to be meteor scars and now thought to be shaped by ocean waves and wind.
Spivey's Corner, near the start, has held a Hollerin' Contest since 1969.
Elizabethtown was the site of the 1781 battle in which Whigs drove Tories into a ravine now called Tory Hole.

byways.name: Cherohala Skyway
byways.where: NC 143 from Santeetlah Gap west of Robbinsville to the Tennessee line (17.8 NC miles); Graham County

facts.fact: Planning began in 1958 and the skyway was completed on October 12, 1996, at a cost of about $100 million; its name joins Cherokee and Nantahala, the two national forests it crosses.
Hooper's Bald, the highest point on the skyway at 5,429 feet, was once a private hunting preserve stocked with buffalo, elk and wild boar; descendants of the boar remain.
An overlook looks down on the Joyce Kilmer Memorial Forest, dedicated in 1936.

byways.name: Clayton Bypass Scenic Byway
byways.where: US 70 Clayton Bypass from I-40 to US 70 Business (9.3 miles); Johnston County

facts.fact: It is one of only two freeways in North Carolina designated as scenic byways.
The route runs 9.3 miles from the I-40 interchange to US 70 Business.
Long straightaways give distant views over the farmland of Johnston County.

byways.name: Colonial Heritage Byway
byways.where: Back roads and US 158, NC 62, NC 86 from near Summerfield through Caswell County (Milton, Yanceyville, Leasburg) and Hillsborough to Durham; Guilford, Rockingham, Caswell, Orange and Durham counties

facts.fact: General Nathanael Greene retreated to the Troublesome Creek Ironworks after Guilford Court House in 1781, and Washington visited ten years later.
Before the Civil War, Milton had two newspapers and a branch of the state bank.
Mid-1800s general stores at Hightowers and Prospect Hill on NC 86 are still in use.

byways.name: Crowders Mountain Drive
byways.where: Sparrow Springs Rd and Pinnacle Rd around Crowders Mountain State Park between US 74 and NC 161 near Kings Mountain (8.1 miles); Gaston and Cleveland counties

facts.fact: The byway circles the base of Crowders and Kings mountains.
The Pinnacle, the highest peak of the Kings Mountain Range, has a weathered granite cap called a monadnock.
Crowders Mountain is named for a local settler.

byways.name: Devil's Tramping Ground Road
byways.where: NC 902 from the Pittsboro courthouse through Harpers Crossroads, then Howard Mill Rd to NC 705 (33.4 miles); Chatham, Randolph and Moore counties

facts.fact: The byway is named for a circular bare path in a clearing that, by local legend, the devil wears down with his pacing.
The site is on private property, reached by a side road from Harpers Crossroads and a short path into the woods.
The route passes Round Top Mountain and crosses the Rocky River.

byways.name: Drovers Road
byways.where: US 74A from the Blue Ridge Parkway near Fairview through Hickory Nut Gap and Gerton to Bat Cave (16.9 miles); Buncombe and Henderson counties

facts.fact: Farmers drove market-bound livestock through Hickory Nut Gap, giving the byway its name.
Sherrill's Inn, open from 1834 to 1909, served drovers and travelers and is visible from the road.
Gerton was formerly known as Pump.

byways.name: East Connecticut Avenue
byways.where: East Connecticut Ave (SR 2033) from Southern Pines to the Fort Bragg gate (2.8 miles); Moore County

facts.fact: Weymouth Woods, established in 1963, was the first natural area in the state park system.
The preserve's old-growth longleaf pines range from 250 to 450 years old, including a pine dating from 1548.
The byway ends at the entrance to Fort Bragg.

byways.name: Edenton-Windsor Loop
byways.where: A figure-eight from Edenton via US 17, NC 45, the Sans Souci ferry, Windsor, NC 308 and the Albemarle Sound bridge back to Edenton (78 miles); Chowan, Bertie and Washington counties

facts.fact: The Sans Souci Cable Ferry across the Cashie River is one of the last two-car, cable-operated ferries in the state.
The Chowan River is nearly two miles wide at the crossing, with old seine-fishing poles visible near shore at low water.
Penelope Barker and 51 other Edenton women signed a resolve against English tea on October 25, 1774.

byways.name: Flint Hill Ramble
byways.where: Flint Hill Rd from Ophir Rd to Love Joy Rd in the Uwharrie National Forest (4.4 miles); Montgomery County

facts.fact: The area was settled during the mid-1800s gold boom; Ophir is named for the Biblical source of Solomon's gold.
The route passes the northern trailhead of the 20-mile Uwharrie National Recreation Trail.
Jumping Off Rock, a bluff over a cascading stream, is about a quarter mile east of the trailhead.

byways.name: Fontana Byway
byways.where: NC 28 from Deals Gap past Fontana Dam and Stecoah to Franklin; Swain, Graham and Macon counties

facts.fact: Fontana Dam, built by the Tennessee Valley Authority and completed in 1945, was the highest dam in the eastern United States at the time.
Surge pipes run up the mountainsides around the Stecoah community to store overflow from the hydroelectric dams.
The byway starts at Deals Gap, the curvy stretch known locally as the Tail of the Dragon.

byways.name: Football Road
byways.where: Alamance Church Rd and Greensboro-Chapel Hill Rd from Greensboro through Snow Camp to Carrboro (42 miles); Guilford, Alamance and Orange counties

facts.fact: The road is named for the route Triad fans drove to football games at UNC Chapel Hill.
Snow Camp was settled as a Quaker community in 1749.
Small dairy farms, creeks and ponds line the route, much of which is a designated bicycle route.

byways.name: Forest Heritage Scenic Byway
byways.where: US 276 and NC 215 loop from Brevard through Pisgah National Forest via Woodrow and Lake Logan to Rosman; Transylvania, Haywood and Jackson counties

facts.fact: Looking Glass Falls, a 60-foot waterfall, sits right beside the byway with a pull-off.
The Cradle of Forestry marks the work of Dr. Carl A. Schenck, who began the first forestry school in the United States in 1898.
The byway's highest point is Beech Gap at 5,335 feet, where it meets the Blue Ridge Parkway.

byways.name: French Broad Overview
byways.where: Monticello Rd, NC 251 and US 25/70 Bus from Weaverville along the French Broad River to Marshall (16.3 miles); Buncombe and Madison counties

facts.fact: The road follows old Native American trading paths, with sheer rock palisades lining one side.
Marshall, established in 1852, has only one bridge in town crossing the French Broad River.
Weaverville is home to the Vance Birthplace State Historic Site.

byways.name: Grassy Island Crossing
byways.where: Pinkston River Rd, Grassy Island Rd and NC 109 from near Ansonville across the Pee Dee toward Ellerbe (25.4 miles); Anson and Richmond counties

facts.fact: The byway is named for Grassy Island, earthen masses in the Pee Dee River north of Blewett Falls Lake.
The route passes pine and hardwood forests, swamps and farms along the river.
Pee Dee National Wildlife Refuge, a side trip, is described as North Carolina's only inland wildlife refuge.

byways.name: Green Swamp Byway
byways.where: NC 211 from Supply north through the Green Swamp and Bolton to near Bladenboro (about 52 miles); Brunswick, Columbus and Bladen counties

facts.fact: The byway winds through swamps, pocosins and longleaf pine savannas of the Green Swamp Preserve.
The preserve, almost 17,000 acres, is home to the Venus flytrap, pitcher plants and orchids.
Crusoe Island, an isolated community on the swamp's edge, was founded in 1806 by refugees from French Haiti.

byways.name: Highlands of the Roan Byway
byways.where: NC 80, NC 226 and NC 261 from Micaville through Bakersville to Carvers Gap and the Roan Mountain Rhododendron Gardens; Yancey and Mitchell counties

facts.fact: Penland School of Craft near Bakersville, founded in 1929, has a 420-acre campus of teaching studios.
Roan Mountain has the largest natural gardens of Catawba rhododendron in the world, with the 600-acre gardens blooming in mid to late June.
From Carvers Gap, about 5,500 feet, a 1.7-mile hike reaches Grassy Ridge Bald at 6,189 feet.

byways.name: Historic Flat Rock Byway
byways.where: NC 225, Rutledge Dr, Erkwood Dr and Little River Rd around the village of Flat Rock south of Hendersonville; Henderson County

facts.fact: Flat Rock was a summer haven for wealthy Charlestonians and was known as the Little Charleston of the mountains.
St. John in the Wilderness, a Gothic Revival church built in 1836, is considered the oldest Episcopal church in western North Carolina.
Connemara, built in 1839, was Carl Sandburg's home for 22 years; the house and its dairy goat barn are preserved.

byways.name: Indian Heritage Trail
byways.where: US 220 and NC 73 from Ellerbe past Town Creek Indian Mound to Mount Gilead on NC 731 (22.4 miles); Richmond and Montgomery counties

facts.fact: Town Creek Indian Mound, the oldest North Carolina State Historic Site, was a Pee Dee ceremonial center with reconstructed temples.
North of Ellerbe, US 220 passes through the state's prime peach-growing region with seasonal produce stands.
The Ellerbe Springs Inn is the home of a once-famous mineral spring resort.

byways.name: Interstate 26 Scenic Highway
byways.where: I-26 from Exit 9 at Mars Hill to Sams Gap on the Tennessee line (9 miles); Madison County

facts.fact: Buckner Gap, at nearly 5,000 feet, is the highest point on any interstate in North Carolina.
The Laurel River bridge, 235 feet high, is the tallest in North Carolina and has an automatic de-icing system.
The Appalachian Trail passes under the highway at the state line.

byways.name: Lafayette's Tour
byways.where: From Henderson east through Warrenton, Halifax, Scotland Neck, Murfreesboro and Parker's Ferry to Gatesville and US 158 (170 miles); Vance, Warren, Halifax, Northampton, Hertford, Gates and Pasquotank counties

facts.fact: The byway passes communities Lafayette visited on his 1825 U.S. tour; he spoke in Halifax on February 27, 1825.
The Halifax Resolves, one of the first colonial actions toward independence, were signed in Halifax in 1776.
Parker's Cable Ferry, one of the last two-car ferries in the state, has crossed the Meherrin River since the early 1900s.

byways.name: Little Parkway
byways.where: US 221 (the Yonahlossee Trail) from Linville along Grandfather Mountain to Blowing Rock (18.5 miles); Avery, Caldwell and Watauga counties

facts.fact: The road was built in 1889 by men and mules as a toll road, known as the Yonahlossee Trail.
The Linn Cove Viaduct, visible from the road on Grandfather Mountain, was built from the top down to protect the mountainside.
Blowing Rock is named for a cliff over the Johns River Valley where rising air blows light objects back.

byways.name: McAuley Road Scenic Byway
byways.where: McAuley Rd from Huntersville-Concord Rd to NC 73 (1.6 miles, unpaved); Mecklenburg County

facts.fact: McAuley Road is a 1.6-mile completely unpaved gravel road.
A one-lane wooden bridge crosses Ramah Creek about halfway along.
The Catawba Lands Conservancy protects 775 acres around the road through conservation easements.

byways.name: Mill Bridge Scenic Byway
byways.where: Sherrills Ford Rd, NC 801, Kerr Mill Rd, Millbridge Rd and NC 150 west of Salisbury around Mount Ulla; Rowan County

facts.fact: The byway is named for the flourmill built by Dr. Samuel Kerr in 1823; Kerr Mill is now a museum.
Thyatira Church in the Scotch-Irish settlement of Millbridge is one of the state's oldest Presbyterian churches.
Mount Ulla has what the guide calls the largest community barn quilt in the U.S.

byways.name: Mission Crossing
byways.where: NC 194 and Old Turnpike Rd from near Cranberry through Banner Elk and Valle Crucis to Vilas; Avery and Watauga counties

facts.fact: The Mast General Store in Valle Crucis opened in 1882.
Old Turnpike Road began as a game trail and was a 19th-century toll road; during the Civil War it served the Underground Railroad.
The byway is named for the Valle Crucis Episcopal Mission; Valle Crucis means Vale of the Cross.

byways.name: Mt. Mitchell Scenic Drive
byways.where: NC 128 from the Mount Mitchell summit, the Blue Ridge Parkway, NC 80 and US 19/19E via Micaville and Burnsville to I-26 at Mars Hill; Yancey and Madison counties

facts.fact: Mount Mitchell, at 6,684 feet, is the highest peak in the eastern United States.
Burnsville's town square has a statue of Captain Otway Burns and the 1833 Nu-Wray Inn.
Quilt squares hang on barns and businesses as part of the Quilt Trails of Western North Carolina.

byways.name: Nantahala Byway
byways.where: US 74/19/129 from Marble through Andrews and the Nantahala Gorge to Bryson City; Cherokee, Macon, Swain and Jackson counties

facts.fact: The Cherokee called the Nantahala Gorge the Land of the Midday Sun for its deep valley and steep walls; rafters run it from mid-March to mid-November.
Marble, founded in 1911, is named for the nearby marble deposit, the largest in the state.
The Great Smoky Mountains Railroad runs through the gorge parallel to US 74.

byways.name: New River Valley Byway
byways.where: NC 194 north from Boone through Todd, then US 221 through West Jefferson and NC 88 to Laurel Springs; Watauga and Ashe counties

facts.fact: NC 194 follows what was once called the Old Buffalo Trail.
The New River is believed to be North America's oldest river and flows north.
West Jefferson has a cheese factory on Main Street, described as the only one in the state.

byways.name: Newfound Gap Road Scenic Byway
byways.where: US 441 from the Blue Ridge Parkway near Cherokee to Newfound Gap on the Tennessee line (16.5 NC miles); Swain County

facts.fact: Mingus Mill is an 1886 turbine mill that ground corn and wheat for over 50 years and is run in summer as a historical exhibit.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated Great Smoky Mountains National Park at Newfound Gap in 1940; the Rockefeller Memorial stands there.
The Oconaluftee River parallels part of the byway, and the Mountain Farm Museum's pioneer buildings stand beside the visitor center.

byways.name: North Durham Country Byway
byways.where: Old Oxford Rd, Bahama Rd, Red Mountain Rd, US 501 and S Lowell Rd through Bahama and Rougemont, north Durham County (31 miles)

facts.fact: Stagville, a state historic site, was once among the largest plantation holdings in the South.
Bahama takes its name from the first letters of the Ball, Harris and Mangum families.
Bahama Road passes Lake Michie.

byways.name: Outer Banks National Scenic Byway
byways.where: NC 12 from Whalebone Junction down Bodie, Pea, Hatteras and Ocracoke islands, by ferry to Cedar Island, then US 70 through Atlantic, Sea Level and Smyrna to Beaufort; Dare, Hyde and Carteret counties

facts.fact: Near the community of Atlantic, old workboats fill Atlantic Harbor, a village with a commercial fishing heritage.
The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, built in 1870 and 208 feet tall, is the tallest masonry lighthouse in the United States.
The route takes the free Hatteras Inlet ferry and the roughly 2.25-hour Cedar Island ferry across Pamlico Sound.

byways.name: Pacolet River Byway
byways.where: US 176 from the South Carolina line at Tryon through Saluda to the Henderson County line (11 miles); Polk County

facts.fact: The road crosses the Pacolet River several times and parallels the Saluda Grade, the steepest standard-gauge mainline railway grade in the U.S., opened in 1878.
The route passes through the Tryon Thermal Belt, a microclimate ordinarily free of dew and frost.
Downtown Tryon's Nina Simone Plaza has a 2010 bronze of the Tryon-born singer.

byways.name: Pamlico Scenic Byway
byways.where: From Washington through Bath and Belhaven, then US 264 past Swan Quarter, Engelhard and Stumpy Point to Manns Harbor (122 miles); Beaufort, Hyde and Dare counties

facts.fact: Bath, settled in 1690, is North Carolina's oldest incorporated town, and its St. Thomas Church of 1734 is the oldest church in the state.
Past Belhaven and Scranton, canals and trees form a seven-mile tunnel along the road.
Engelhard is the last stop for fuel or restrooms for about 40 miles, to Manns Harbor; red wolves may be seen in the Alligator River refuge.

byways.name: Pee Dee Valley Drive
byways.where: Valley Dr, NC 24/27/73 and Indian Mound Rd from Badin to Norwood along the Pee Dee River (14.6 miles); Stanly County

facts.fact: Badin was established in 1913 around a French-built aluminum plant; ALCOA finished the dam and has run it since 1917.
Badin's French-inspired townhouses are among the earliest townhouse architecture in North Carolina.
Morrow Mountain State Park, a side trip, looks over Badin Lake and Lake Tillery.

byways.name: Perquimans Crossing
byways.where: US 17 Business / Church St through Hertford across the Perquimans River (2 miles); Perquimans County

facts.fact: The road enters Hertford on an S-shaped swing bridge over the Perquimans River, believed to be the only one of its kind still operating in the nation.
The Perquimans County courthouse holds the Durant Deed of 1661, the oldest deed on record in North Carolina.
The Newbold-White House, built about 1730, is a short side trip on Church Street.

byways.name: Pisgah Loop Byway
byways.where: NC 181, NC 183, Old NC 105 through Linville Gorge, NC 126 and Fish Hatchery Rd, a loop northwest of Morganton; Burke County

facts.fact: About 15 miles of the loop are unpaved along the Linville Gorge Wilderness, and four-wheel drive is required there.
Wiseman's View overlooks Table Rock, Hawksbill Mountain and the Linville River in the gorge far below.
The Linville access area at Lake James was a filming site for The Last of the Mohicans.

byways.name: Pottery Road
byways.where: NC 705 from Eagle Springs through Robbins, Whynot and Jugtown to Seagrove (25.3 miles); Moore and Randolph counties

facts.fact: Seven families from Staffordshire, England, settled here in the 18th century, and their descendants still make pottery; nearly 80 potteries lie near the route.
Old cedars line the first stretch of NC 705, known locally as Cedar Lane.
Whynot got its name because residents could not agree on a name for the post office.

byways.name: Roanoke Voyages Corridor
byways.where: US 64 (Old Hwy 64) across Roanoke Island through Manteo from the Manns Harbor bridge to the Washington Baum Bridge (6.8 miles); Dare County

facts.fact: Roanoke Island was the site of the first English settlement in North America, the Lost Colony.
The outdoor drama The Lost Colony, the state's longest-running, plays at the Waterside Theater.
Roanoke Island Festival Park in Manteo is home of the Elizabeth II, a restored 16th-century vessel.

byways.name: Rolling Kansas Byway
byways.where: S Main St / Millingport Rd and Bear Creek Church Rd from Richfield to the Cabarrus line (9.2 miles); Stanly County

facts.fact: The area was nicknamed Rolling Kansas for its hilly terrain and its turn-of-the-century farms and windmills.
The graveyard at Bethel Bear Creek United Church of Christ has tombstones from the 1820s and is among the oldest in Stanly County.
The route runs 9.2 miles from Richfield to the Cabarrus County line.

byways.name: Sandhills Scenic Drive
byways.where: NC 24/27 west from Carthage through Biscoe and Troy across the Pee Dee to Albemarle (46.2 miles); Moore, Montgomery and Stanly counties

facts.fact: Scottish highlanders settled the Sandhills about 1740; the region is named for its coarse sandy soil.
Horse Trough and Shelter mountains of the Uwharrie range are visible on either side as the road nears the Pee Dee.
Troy sits on the eastern edge of the Uwharrie National Forest, near the 20-mile Uwharrie Trail.

byways.name: Sauratown Mountains Scenic Byway
byways.where: NC 89, NC 66 and back roads from Mount Airy through Danbury and Hanging Rock State Park around to Pilot Mountain State Park; Surry and Stokes counties

facts.fact: Mount Airy, Andy Griffith's hometown, inspired the fictional Mayberry.
The Moratock Iron Furnace in Danbury, built of granite blocks in 1843, made swords and munitions for the Confederacy.
The byway makes a full loop around the base of Pilot Mountain, whose Big Pinnacle is a quartzite monadnock once used as a landmark by the Saura people.

byways.name: Scots-Welsh Heritage Byway
byways.where: Old NC 86, Arthur Minnis Rd, Orange Grove Rd, Dairyland Rd and Rocky Ridge Rd south of Hillsborough (13.2 miles); Orange County

facts.fact: Old NC 86 appears on colonial maps dating to 1770.
Dairyland Road was originally part of a Native American trading path.
Maple View Country Store at Dairyland and Rocky Ridge roads is known for homemade ice cream.

byways.name: South Mountain Scenery
byways.where: NC 226 north from the Metcalf community near Shelby through Polkville to Marion (34 miles); Cleveland, Rutherford and McDowell counties

facts.fact: The byway follows NC 226 for 34 miles from near Shelby to Marion.
Corn fields and apple orchards line the route as it leaves the Piedmont for the mountains.
Cherry Mountain got its name from the cherry bounce liquor brewed from local cherries after the Civil War.

byways.name: Tar Heel Trace
byways.where: NC 42, NC 124, NC 142 and NC 125 from Wilson through Conetoe to Williamston (51.7 miles); Wilson, Edgecombe and Martin counties

facts.fact: The byway takes its name from the pine tar industry that once thrived in the region.
Conetoe, incorporated in 1887 and pronounced Cuh-knee-ta, is surrounded by soybean and peanut fields.
Sheds and silos near Williamston store peanuts, one of the region's dominant crops.

byways.name: The College Town Ride
byways.where: NC 115 (Main St) through Davidson, then Concord Rd, Grey Rd and Shearer Rd to Fisher Farm Park (5.5 miles); Iredell and Mecklenburg counties

facts.fact: Davidson College was founded by Presbyterian farmers in 1837, and the college arboretum covers the campus.
The Helper Hotel (1848) on Main Street began as a store and became a hotel for college visitors.
A campus marker notes that physics professor Henry Louis Smith developed the first X-ray machine in the U.S. in 1896.

byways.name: Turkey Creek Byway
byways.where: US 264 east from the Zebulon area to the Wilson County line (11 miles); Nash County

facts.fact: About 2,500 feet of Turkey Creek flows through the highway's wide median.
In the early 1970s NCDOT widened the median of the relocated highway so the creek could keep its natural channel.
The byway runs 11 miles on US 264 from just east of Zebulon to the Wilson County line.

byways.name: U.S. 421 Scenic Highway
byways.where: US 421 from the Blue Ridge Parkway overpass at Deep Gap toward Boone (8.5 miles); Watauga County

facts.fact: Deep Gap was the home of guitarist Doc Watson and his son Merle.
The Blue Ridge Parkway crosses US 421 near the start on a bridge faced with native stone.
Fraser fir Christmas tree farms are visible along the way; Watauga County is a leading national producer.

byways.name: Upper Yadkin Way
byways.where: NC 268 from US 321 north of Lenoir through Happy Valley, Ferguson and Goshen to Wilkesboro (26.3 miles); Caldwell and Wilkes counties

facts.fact: The route follows the Yadkin River from the mountains into the foothills through Happy Valley.
Fort Defiance near Patterson is the restored 1790 house of General William Lenoir.
W. Kerr Scott Reservoir at Goshen was formed in 1962.

byways.name: Uwharrie Scenic Road
byways.where: NC 49 from Asheboro through the Uwharrie Mountains to near Concord, with an NC 109 extension through Denton; Randolph, Davidson, Rowan, Stanly and Cabarrus counties

facts.fact: The route crosses the Carolina Slate Belt, where many buildings and fences were once built of slate.
The Uwharrie Mountains were formed by volcanoes several hundred million years ago.
Reed Gold Mine, a side trip, is the site of the first authenticated gold discovery in the U.S., in 1799.

byways.name: Waterfall Byway
byways.where: US 64 west from Rosman through Cashiers, Highlands and Franklin to Murphy; Transylvania, Jackson, Macon, Clay and Cherokee counties

facts.fact: The byway runs 98 miles through five western counties.
Bridal Veil Falls outside Highlands is 45 feet tall and sits about 20 feet from US 64.
The route descends through the Cullasaja Gorge, and Murphy's courthouse is built entirely of local marble.

byways.name: Whitewater Way
byways.where: NC 281 south from Sapphire past Gorges State Park to the South Carolina line (8.7 miles); Jackson and Transylvania counties

facts.fact: Whitewater Falls, 411 feet, is a short walk from the byway.
The route passes Gorges State Park and runs 8.7 miles to the South Carolina line.
Large stands of hemlock and spruce line this part of the route.

byways.name: Yadkin Valley Scenic Byway
byways.where: Back roads from near Mount Airy through Dobson, Rockford, Yadkinville and Elkin along the Yadkin River (76.5 miles); Surry and Yadkin counties

facts.fact: The area was known for tobacco and is turning to vineyards and wineries, including the Swan Creek Wine Trail.
Pilot Mountain, a knob rising 1,400 feet, is visible for much of the route.
The route passes the 1840 Kapp House and the Edwards-Franklin House of 1799.
